title: The Bible Never Said Money Is Evil… But What It Reveals Will Expose Your Heart
paragraphs: The Bible Never Said Money Is Evil… But What It Reveals Will Expose Your Heart
You’ve probably heard it your whole life… whispered in sermons, thrown around in conversations, even used to shame success…
“Money is the root of all evil.”
But something about that never sat right, did it?
Because deep down, you’ve seen good people with money… and broken people without it.
So what if I told you the Bible never actually said that?
Not once.
The verse everyone quotes comes from 1 Timothy 6:10, and in the original Greek, it reads:

“ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία”
(rhiza gar pantōn tōn kakōn estin hē philargyria)
Which translates accurately to:
“For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.”
Not money.
The love of it.
“φιλαργυρία” (philargyria) literally means an obsessive affection, a deep craving, a devotion to wealth that begins to replace God.
And that’s where everything shifts.
Because now the question isn’t “Is money evil?”
The real question is…
What does your heart do when money enters the room?
Because money doesn’t create your character.
It reveals it.
Jesus Himself said in Luke 16:13:
“No servant can serve two masters… You cannot serve God and mammon.”
That word “mammon” comes from Aramaic — מָמוֹנָא (mamona) — meaning wealth, yes… but more deeply, it carries the idea of that which you trust in.
So this was never just about currency.
It was always about worship.
What do you rely on when life starts shaking?
What do you run to when you feel empty?
What makes you feel safe?
Be honest…
Because if it’s not God, then it’s already become your master.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Money can bless.
Money can build.
Money can feed the hungry, fund ministries, rescue lives, support families, spread the Gospel to places your feet will never touch.
But money can also quietly corrupt… without making a sound.
Judas didn’t betray Jesus for power.
He did it for thirty pieces of silver.
Not because money was evil…
But because his heart loved it more than Christ.
That’s the scandal we don’t talk about enough.
You can walk with Jesus… and still be secretly attached to something else.
You can serve… preach… show up… smile…
And still have something sitting on the throne that doesn’t belong there.
That’s why Scripture goes deeper than behavior.
It goes straight to the heart.
In Matthew 6:21, Jesus says:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
The original Greek word for “treasure” is “θησαυρός” (thēsauros) — not just money, but anything you store up, protect, prioritize, and give value to.
So let’s not pretend this is just about finances.
This is about devotion.
This is about identity.
This is about what owns you when no one is watching.
Because the truth is…
Some people don’t have money, but money still has them.
And others have wealth, but it doesn’t have their heart.
That’s the difference.
Abraham was rich.
David had wealth.
Solomon had unimaginable riches.
Yet when their hearts were aligned with God, their resources became instruments of purpose, not idols of destruction.
But when Solomon’s heart drifted…
The same wealth that once reflected God’s blessing became entangled with idolatry.
So again… it’s not the money.
It’s the heart holding it.
And if you’re reading this right now, something in you probably stirred.
Maybe conviction.
Maybe recognition.
Maybe a quiet discomfort you can’t ignore.
Be honest…
Have you ever trusted money more than God?
Have you ever felt safer with a full bank account than with a full prayer life?
Have you ever delayed obedience because of financial fear?
Because this isn’t about shame.
This is about freedom.
Jesus never came to take from you.
He came to free you.
Free you from the silent chains that don’t look like sin on the outside… but slowly pull your heart away from Him.
He came to rewrite your story.
Even the parts you thought were too entangled.
Even the parts where money became your security, your identity, your escape.
Because grace doesn’t just forgive…
It transforms.
Zacchaeus was a wealthy tax collector, known for corruption.
But one encounter with Jesus…
And everything changed.
He didn’t just say sorry.
He gave back what he stole.
He surrendered his wealth’s control over him.
That’s what real transformation looks like.
Not just belief.
But release.
So the question isn’t “Do you have money?”
The question is…
Does money have you?
And if it does…
Jesus is still inviting you out of that prison.
Not with condemnation.
But with grace.
If this message spoke to you, don’t keep it to yourself.
Because this is more than content.
This is discipleship.
If you want to glorify God not just with words but with action…
Support what feeds your spirit.
Stay connected to truth.
Commit to growth.
Because following Jesus isn’t about avoiding evil…
It’s about surrendering everything that quietly replaces Him.
And maybe the most dangerous idols…
Are the ones we’ve learned to justify.
Let this be the moment you stop pretending and start surrendering.
Because what you cling to…
Might be the very thing keeping you from freedom.
